title: A Stronger Europe in a Weaker Transatlantic Order
content: Transatlantic relations have always moved between cooperation and crisis. The Iraq War deeply divided Europe and the US, trade disputes have strained relations, and Trump’s first presidency brought open conflict over NATO, burden-sharing and multilateral cooperation. Yet shared interests, strong economic ties, common institutions and a basic commitment to liberal democracy remained in place even when governments disagreed, allowing the partners to manage disagreements over individual policies within a broader and strong relationship.

title: An Uneasy Transatlantic Truce
content:
The second Trump administration has done significant damage to the transatlantic relationship, which is now marked by suspicion and frustration. The economic side of the relationship is no exception. After the dramatic disruption of Liberation Day, when President Trump announced the imposition of unlawful 20% tariffs on imports from the European Union, the EU and the US negotiated their way to a truce that has now been in place for a bit over a year.

The terms of the truce are lopsided. Under the framework agreed at Turnberry in July 2025, the United States applied a 15% ceiling, inclusive of existing duties, to most imports from the EU, though steel, aluminum, and copper stayed at 50%. The EU, for its part, agreed to eliminate its tariffs on American industrial goods, open its market to a list of agricultural and seafood products, and shelve the €93 billion package of countermeasures it had prepared. The average American tariff on European goods, below 2% a year earlier, is now close to 10%; the average European tariff on American goods approaches zero. Europe accepted this agreement—inconceivable just a year earlier—as the price of stability.

title: No More Rules: The End of the Transatlantic Alliance?
content: The Transatlantic relationship relies on the rules-based international order established by the US and Western Allies after the Second World War. Rules, however, no longer apply to the behaviour of the United States under President Trump. His approach is purely transactional, and he does not believe in mutually beneficial alliances. He thinks that Europe and Canada have been ‘ripping off’ the US and now must pay for it. His administration is systematically neutering international bodies, for example by sanctioning judges of the International Criminal Court. Former Estonian President Lennart Meri quipped that international law is the nuclear weapon of small states. Trump, however, is returning the world to the law of jungle where weaker countries are vulnerable to larger predators.

title: Dealing with an Influential Ally
content: European public discussion about foreign political influence has developed around a familiar distinction. Adversaries, particularly Russia, are often covertly but demonstrably seeking to shape European politics from within. Allies, above all the United States, are partners with whom disagreements are managed through diplomacy – even if it is often conducted away from public scrutiny. Under the second Trump administration, this distinction has become increasingly difficult to maintain. Washington has not merely disagreed with European governments over defence spending, trade, Greenland, or Ukraine. It has increasingly taken sides in political conflicts within EU member states. Importantly, the dominant Trump administration narrative – defending freedom of speech and the will of the people against odious liberal elites – increasingly aligns with how the Kremlin justifies its political influence campaigns in Europe. Three recent cases from this year illustrate both the differences in how the two powers exert influence transnationally and the alignment of their near-term political goals in Europe.

title: Transatlanticism from Within
content:
Donald Trump’s transactional pursuit of US primacy and strongly nationalistic outlook have prompted a reappraisal of relations with Europe among US foreign policy thinkers, while the uncertain standing of US security commitments has prompted similar processes in Europe.

Such debates have in fact extended beyond the narrow remit of the foreign policy establishment into the political arena. Politics has thus acquired renewed centrality in transatlantic exchanges, so much so that the future of the US-European alliance will be severely affected by how ideological imperatives will be reconciled with the hard realities of geopolitics and economic security.
